title: HE SENT AWAY TWO WIVES… THEN THE BIBLE RECORDED THE CHILDREN HE HAD WITH ANOTHER WOMAN.
paragraphs: HE SENT AWAY TWO WIVES… THEN THE BIBLE RECORDED THE CHILDREN HE HAD WITH ANOTHER WOMAN.

Buried in a genealogy most Christians skip is the unsettling story of Shaharaim—a man with a complicated household, two women sent away, and a family history Scripture refuses to erase. But what does this ancient record actually reveal about marriage, brokenness, consequences, and the grace of Jesus Christ?
“And Shaharaim begat children in the country of Moab, after he had sent them away; Hushim and Baara were his wives.” — 1 Chronicles 8:8 (KJV)
There are some Bible verses that make you stop reading.
Not because they contain a spectacular miracle.
Not because an angel appeared, a sea opened, or fire fell from heaven.
But because they sound painfully familiar.
A man. Two wives. A separation. Another woman. More children.
And somewhere behind those few ancient words, a household whose full story we will never know.
Imagine being one of the people whose entire family history was reduced to a sentence.
No explanation of what went wrong.
No account of who cried.
No record of who left willingly, who felt abandoned, or what the children understood.
Just names.
And a sentence that has survived thousands of years.
He sent them away.
Before we go any further, there is something important we must understand.
The Bible does not tell us that Shaharaim was a hero for doing this.
It does not tell us that God commanded him to send those women away.
It does not tell us that his later children were a divine reward for his decisions.
And it certainly does not give anyone permission to discard a spouse when marriage becomes difficult.
Scripture records what happened without necessarily approving what happened.
That distinction matters more than many people realize.
Because sometimes the most dangerous thing we can do with the Bible is take a man's behavior and call it God's blessing simply because his story appears in a sacred book.
And sometimes the most beautiful thing we can discover is that God allowed a deeply complicated human history to remain in His Word without pretending it was simple.
The man's name was Shaharaim.
His story appears in 1 Chronicles 8, in the genealogy of Benjamin.
Not in a dramatic chapter filled with dialogue.
Not in a story where we hear God's voice explaining every decision.
In a genealogy.
The kind of passage many of us hurry through because the names are difficult to pronounce and the details seem distant from our lives.
But slow down.
Because there is something unsettling here.
The Hebrew of 1 Chronicles 8:8 includes the phrase:
אַחֲרֵי שִׁלְחוֹ אֹתָם
ʾaḥărê shilləḥô ʾōtām
Meaning, in context, “after he had sent them away.”
The Hebrew verb comes from the root שׁלח (š-l-ḥ), meaning “to send” or “to send away.”
The text uses language of sending away, but it does not explain every legal or personal circumstance surrounding the separation.
That is important.

Some English translations, including the King James Version, identify Hushim and Baara as Shaharaim's wives in this verse. Other translations reflect the difficulty of the Hebrew wording and its relationship to the surrounding genealogy.
The passage is ancient, compressed, and not without interpretive challenges.
We should not pretend to know what the Holy Spirit has not revealed.
We cannot confidently reconstruct the conversations inside Shaharaim's household.
We cannot prove why the women were sent away.
We cannot say whether either woman was mistreated, whether there were legal divorces, or what motives governed Shaharaim's decisions.
But we can say this:
The biblical record preserves a complicated family history without giving us permission to romanticize it.
And perhaps that is exactly where some of us need to begin.
Because there are people reading this who know what it means to have a family story they would rather not explain.
Maybe you grew up in a house where one parent disappeared.
Maybe you watched a marriage collapse while everyone outside the home thought everything was fine.
Maybe you were the child from the second relationship.
The person introduced with an awkward pause.
The one who learned too early that adults can make decisions children must spend years trying to understand.
Or perhaps you are the person who made those decisions.
You hurt someone.
You walked away when you should have stayed and sought help.
You made promises you did not keep.
And now, years later, the consequences still have names, birthdays, memories, and faces.
There is a kind of pain that does not disappear just because life continues.
And that is why this little genealogy deserves our attention.
Because life continued for Shaharaim, too.
First Chronicles 8:9–10 records children associated with Hodesh, another woman named in his household:
Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, Malcam, Jeuz, Shachia, and Mirma.
The Hebrew of verse 9 begins:
וַיּוֹלֶד מִן־חֹדֶשׁ אִשְׁתּוֹ
wayyôled min-Ḥōdeš ʾištô
That is, “And he fathered [children] by Hodesh his wife.”
The genealogy then continues, mentioning additional sons connected with Hushim in verse 11.
Notice something.
Hushim has not simply vanished from the record.
Even after the language about sending away, her name remains connected with Shaharaim's family history.
The exact chronology and relationships are not fully explained, and verse 11 is another reason to read the passage carefully rather than invent a tidy narrative.
These are not merely decorative details.
They remind us that a genealogy can preserve relationships whose complexity we do not completely understand.
And here is where the story begins to reach beyond the ancient world.
A new chapter in someone's life does not automatically erase the responsibilities of the previous one.
A new marriage does not make past children irrelevant.
A new relationship does not cancel old wounds.
A new beginning is not the same thing as repentance.
And having more children is not, by itself, proof that God approves of every decision that came before them.
Some people confuse continued life with divine endorsement.
But the Bible never teaches that every person who prospers is righteous, or that every person who suffers has sinned.
Jesus directly challenged simplistic assumptions about suffering and guilt in John 9:1–3.
The presence of children is a gift of life, not a certificate declaring every parental decision holy.
And this is especially important when we talk about families.
Because children are never the scandal.
A child born into a complicated family is not a mistake.
A child conceived outside God's design for marriage does not inherit the moral guilt of the circumstances surrounding conception.
Every human being bears the dignity of being made in God's image (Genesis 1:26–27).
No one should have to spend their life apologizing for the circumstances of their birth.
Read that again if you need to.
You are not responsible for the decisions adults made before you could speak.
You may carry consequences you never chose.
You may have questions no one has answered.
You may still feel the ache of being overlooked, compared, abandoned, or treated as though you belonged to the wrong chapter of somebody else's life.
But your worth was never determined by the neatness of your family tree.
And the Gospel gives us an even deeper reason to hope.
Because Jesus Christ entered a world full of complicated family histories.
Matthew opens his Gospel with a genealogy.
And that genealogy does not hide every uncomfortable detail.
Judah and Tamar appear in the story behind Matthew 1:3.
Rahab is named in Matthew 1:5.
Ruth, a Moabite woman whose loyalty and faith became part of Israel's story, is named there too.
And in Matthew 1:6, Solomon's mother is identified through the painful history of David and Uriah.
These accounts are not identical to Shaharaim's story.
We should never flatten their differences.
But together they reveal something remarkable about the biblical witness.
God does not need a sanitized human history to accomplish His redemptive purposes.
He does not call betrayal faithfulness.
He does not rename adultery righteousness.
He does not excuse injustice because a powerful man committed it.
Yet human sin does not have the power to overthrow God's purposes.
Think about David.
The king who wrote beautiful psalms also committed grievous sins.
He took Bathsheba, another man's wife, and arranged for Uriah's death (2 Samuel 11).
The prophet Nathan confronted him.
David was not told that his royal position made him innocent.
He was not told that because God had chosen him, his actions no longer mattered.
He heard the words:
“Thou art the man.” — 2 Samuel 12:7 (KJV)
And suddenly, the king could no longer hide behind his throne.
That is one of the hardest mercies God can give us.
To expose what we have been defending.
To confront what we have been excusing.
To reveal that we cannot heal what we insist on hiding.
David eventually confessed:
“I have sinned against the LORD.” — 2 Samuel 12:13 (KJV)
That confession did not remove every earthly consequence.
Forgiveness was real.
Consequences were real.
Both truths stood together.
And perhaps that is what someone reading this needs to hear.
Grace is not permission to repeat the wound.
Forgiveness is not an instruction to pretend nothing happened.
Repentance is not simply feeling emotional because you were caught.
Biblical repentance involves turning toward God and away from sin, with a transformed direction of life.
The Greek New Testament uses the word μετάνοια (metanoia), commonly translated “repentance.”
It speaks of a change of mind and orientation, not merely temporary regret.
When Peter called people to repent in Acts 3:19, he was calling them to turn toward God.
And when John the Baptist spoke about repentance, he demanded fruit consistent with it (Matthew 3:8).
That means a person who has harmed a family cannot simply say, “God forgave me,” while refusing to take responsibility for the damage.
Where possible and appropriate, repentance seeks to tell the truth, make restitution, fulfill obligations, and pursue reconciliation without demanding that wounded people immediately trust again.
Sometimes that includes financial responsibility.
Sometimes it means acknowledging children who were neglected.
Sometimes it means ending deception.
Sometimes it means respecting boundaries and allowing the people you hurt to heal without controlling their process.
And sometimes repentance means accepting that forgiveness does not guarantee the restoration of a particular relationship.
God's mercy is not a weapon to force someone back into an unsafe situation.
That is not grace.
That is spiritual manipulation.
Jesus never taught us to use holy language to cover unholy behavior.
When religious leaders questioned Him about divorce, He took them back to God's design for marriage.
In Matthew 19:4–6, Jesus pointed to creation, to the union of husband and wife, and to the seriousness of what God joins together.
He also explained that Moses permitted divorce because of hardness of heart (Matthew 19:8).
Jesus did not treat marriage as something disposable.
He did not teach that a person's desire for a new beginning automatically justified abandoning an existing covenant.
His teaching confronts the human tendency to make our own desires the final authority.
At the same time, biblical teaching on marriage must never be twisted into a demand that victims remain exposed to violence, coercion, or abuse.
The seriousness of marriage does not make cruelty holy.
Protecting the vulnerable is not rebellion against God.
And seeking safety is not the same thing as treating marriage lightly.
We must handle these passages with reverence, compassion, and care.
Because somewhere reading this is a person who has already been crushed by careless religious advice.
Someone who was told to endure what should have been confronted.
Someone whose suffering was dismissed because the person causing it knew how to quote Scripture.
And somewhere else is a person who needs to stop calling selfishness freedom.
Both need truth.
Both need the Gospel.
But they do not need the same confrontation.
Jesus knows the difference.
Remember the woman at the well in John 4.
Jesus told her that she had had five husbands and that the man she was then living with was not her husband.
We are not given enough information to know all the reasons behind those earlier marriages.
We should not invent a history of promiscuity or blame where Scripture does not provide it.
But we do know that Jesus knew the truth about her circumstances.
And He still spoke with her.
He did not flatter her with a lie.
He did not reduce her to her relationship history.
He offered her living water.
He spoke of worship in spirit and truth.
And He revealed Himself as the Messiah.
There is something breathtaking about that encounter.
The One who knew her life most completely was the One who could offer her what no human relationship could provide.
Not another temporary escape.
Not another person expected to carry the weight of her deepest thirst.
Living water.
The gift of God.
And she went back to her town with a testimony that invited others to come and see Jesus.
Her story was no longer simply something to conceal.
It became an occasion to point people toward Christ.
That is not because the past stopped mattering.
It is because Jesus was greater than the past.
And this is where Shaharaim's brief genealogy becomes a mirror.
Not because we know enough to condemn every decision he made.
We do not.
Not because we can prove that his household followed the same pattern as every broken modern family.
We cannot.
But because the passage reminds us that Scripture does not erase the complicated reality of human relationships.
And when we read that reality in the light of the whole Bible, we are confronted with questions we cannot easily escape.
What have we called normal that God is calling us to examine?
Whose pain have we ignored because our own life became more comfortable?
Have we confused being forgiven with being free from responsibility?
Have we allowed bitterness to become our identity?
Have we started believing that the circumstances of our birth determine the value of our lives?
Have we treated someone's past as though Jesus could never redeem them?
And perhaps the hardest question of all:
Are we asking God to heal our story while refusing to surrender the part of it we still want to control?
That question is not only for divorced people.
It is not only for parents.
It is not only for those who have experienced betrayal.
It is for all of us.
Because every human heart knows something about wanting mercy without exposure.
We want Jesus to forgive the sin we are still protecting.
We want peace without confession.
We want restoration without humility.
We want a beautiful testimony without the painful honesty that often comes before it.
But Jesus did not go to the cross merely to make us feel better about remaining unchanged.
He came to save sinners.
He came to reconcile us to God.
He came to free us from the dominion of sin.
He came to make us new.
The apostle Paul wrote:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17 (KJV)
Notice where that promise is found.
In Christ.
Not in a new relationship.
Not in a different city.
Not in a better public image.
Not in pretending the past never happened.
In Christ.
And that changes everything.
Because the deepest human problem is not merely that our families are complicated.
It is that sin has separated humanity from the holy God who made us.
Romans 3:23 tells us that all have sinned and fall short of God's glory.
Romans 6:23 tells us that the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.
And Romans 5:8 declares that God demonstrated His love toward us while we were still sinners, through Christ's death for us.
The Gospel is not the announcement that our actions have no consequences.

It is the announcement that Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, died for sinners and rose again, so that those who repent and believe in Him may receive forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and new life.
He does not merely edit the public version of our story.
He transforms the person at its center.
And sometimes that transformation begins with a sentence we have been afraid to say.
“I was wrong.”
“I need forgiveness.”
“I hurt people.”
“I cannot keep living like this.”
“Jesus, I need You.”
Or perhaps:
“Lord, I have spent years believing that what happened to me made me unworthy of love.”
And in the presence of Christ, that lie begins to lose its grip.
Because your family's history may explain some of your wounds.
But it does not have the authority to define your eternal worth.
Your father may have left.
Your mother may have struggled.
Your marriage may have ended.
Your children may be carrying pain you deeply regret.
Your life may contain chapters you wish you could rewrite.
But no human failure can make the saving power of Jesus insufficient.
And no amount of religious performance can replace the need for His grace.
That is why we must be careful with the phrase “From Scandal to Grace.”
It does not mean scandal is good.
It does not mean every broken relationship should be celebrated as a stepping stone toward something better.
It does not mean every painful decision was secretly God's command.
It means that even where sin, shame, sorrow, and brokenness have entered the human story, the grace of Jesus Christ is sufficient to forgive, restore, and transform those who come to Him.
The cross does not excuse the scandal.
The cross reveals how seriously God takes sin—and how astonishingly far His love went to save sinners.
And the resurrection declares that death and sin do not have the final victory over those who belong to Christ.
That is the hope.
Not that every earthly relationship will be repaired exactly as we wish.
Not that every person we hurt will return.
Not that every painful memory will disappear overnight.
But that Jesus is alive.
That repentance is possible.
That forgiveness is available through Him.
That healing can begin.
And that the future of a redeemed person is not imprisoned by the worst chapter of the past.
Perhaps you have been reading this with a particular name in your mind.
A father.
A mother.
An ex-spouse.
A child.
Someone who left.
Someone you abandoned.
Someone you still cannot forgive.
Or perhaps the name is your own.
Not to pretend everything is simple.
Not to manufacture an emotion.
But to ask Jesus to lead you in truth.
If you need to repent, repent.
If you need to seek help, seek help.
If you need to make something right, begin where you can.
If you need to grieve, do not mistake grief for a lack of faith.
And if you have been carrying guilt for decisions that were never yours, ask the Lord to help you lay down that burden.
You do not need to confess somebody else's sin as though it were your own.
You need the Savior who knows your story completely.
There may be someone reading this who has never genuinely surrendered to Jesus Christ.
You know Christian language.
You know how to appear strong.
You may even know how to encourage other people.
But when you are alone, you know there are places in your heart you have never opened to Him.
Today, you can come honestly.
You do not have to make yourself worthy before approaching Christ.
You come because you need His mercy.
Confess your sin.
Turn to Him.
Trust in His death and resurrection.
Follow Him as Lord.
And remember His promise:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37 (KJV)
There is room to come to Christ.
Not room to cherish sin forever.
But room to be forgiven, cleansed, and changed by the Savior.
And for the believer who has grown weary, this is your reminder:
God has not called you to manufacture a perfect-looking life.
He has called you to walk in the light.
To love truth.
To practice mercy.
To pursue holiness.
To carry your responsibilities faithfully.
To forgive as you have been forgiven.
And to keep your eyes on Jesus.
The same Christ who confronted sin also welcomed repentant sinners.
The same Christ who defended the vulnerable also challenged the proud.
The same Christ who spoke with the woman at the well went willingly to the cross.
And the same Christ who rose from the grave remains the hope of every broken human story.
If this article has touched a part of your life you rarely talk about, I want to invite you into something more meaningful than simply reacting to another post.
Be honest before God.
You do not have to reveal private details or expose anyone else's pain.
Sometimes a few honest words are enough to remind another struggling believer that they are not alone.
And please, think about the person who might need this message.
The friend who still blames themselves for their parents' separation.
The single mother who wonders whether her family can ever find peace.
The father trying to rebuild trust after years of regret.
The young adult who believes their birth circumstances made them less valuable.
The believer who has confused grace with permission to avoid repentance.
Invite your family, your friends, believers who are growing weary, those who have drifted from the faith, and even those who do not yet believe.
Not because we are building a following around ourselves.
But because the Word of God deserves to be heard, understood, and lived.
There is a real difference between enjoying Christian content when it appears on your feed and intentionally helping make ongoing biblical discipleship resources available to more people.
For some supporters, this may be part of their broader Christian giving—a voluntary offering of gratitude and partnership in Gospel work.
But I want to be clear about something important.
God is not selling grace.
Salvation cannot be purchased.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
If you cannot, you are still welcome here.
You can still pray, learn, grow, share the Word, and encourage others.
Because the mission is bigger than a transaction.
It is about Christ being proclaimed and people being strengthened in the truth.
These items are not the heart of the ministry.
Jesus is.
But they can serve as reminders of Scripture, encouragement in daily life, and opportunities to begin meaningful conversations about faith.
One thoughtful comment might encourage someone to seek prayer.
One invitation might help a friend begin reading the Bible again.
We cannot promise what God will do through any single post.
But we can be faithful with the opportunities He places before us.
And faithfulness matters.
Now, before we finish, return with me to that little genealogy.
Shaharaim.
Hushim.
Baara.
Hodesh.
The children whose names were written down.
The relationships we cannot fully reconstruct.
The questions Scripture leaves unanswered.
We began with a man who sent women away.
We end with the Savior who receives repentant sinners.
And that contrast should move us.
Because Shaharaim's record is not a hidden promise that every complicated family will have a perfect earthly ending.
It is a reminder that the Bible speaks about real people, not polished characters designed to make us comfortable.
And when we bring our own complicated histories to the whole counsel of Scripture, we discover a truth more beautiful than pretending everything was fine.
Jesus Christ came into a world that was not fine.
He came among sinners.
He bore our sins.
He died.
He rose again.
And He calls us out of darkness into His marvelous light.
You may not be able to change the names in your family history.
You may not be able to undo every decision.
You may not be able to recover every lost year.
But in Christ, you can stop running from the truth.
You can receive forgiveness.
You can begin walking in obedience.
You can seek healing without denying the wound.
You can take responsibility without surrendering to despair.
And you can trust the Lord with the chapters you cannot repair by your own strength.
Your past may explain the scars you carry, but only Jesus Christ has the authority to write the final verdict over your redeemed life.
